q: What is the FuelEU Maritime surcharge on my sea freight invoice?
title: FuelEU Maritime surcharge explained
short: It is the carrier passing on its cost of meeting FuelEU Maritime, an EU rule since 1 January 2025 that caps the greenhouse gas intensity of energy used by large ships calling at EU ports. Carriers recover cleaner fuel costs or penalties through it. It is a freight cost, separate from the EU ETS surcharge.
audience: Indian exporters and importers shipping to or from EU ports

ul: Ships over 5,000 gross tonnes carrying cargo or passengers to, from and between EU ports.
A limit on the well-to-wake greenhouse gas intensity of energy used on board, against a reference of 91.16 g CO2e per MJ.
The cut starts at 2% in 2025 and tightens in steps to 80% by 2050.
Voyages between an EU and a non-EU port count at 50% of the energy used, so an India to Rotterdam leg is half covered.
Ships that miss the limit pay a penalty; companies can bank surpluses or pool ships to meet it.

sections.h: How it differs from the EU ETS surcharge
p: The EU ETS line pays for allowances covering the CO2 a ship emits. The FuelEU line pays for the fuel standard: buying biofuel or LNG blends, or the penalty for not doing so. A ship can owe both. Each carrier names and prices them differently, so read the tariff notice for each.

sections.h: Questions to ask your carrier or forwarder
ol: Is the charge per container or per tonne, and on which legs?
Is it based on the fleet's actual compliance position, a pooled position or a flat estimate?
How often is it revised, and is it already inside an all-in rate?
Can you get shipment-level emissions data that reflects the cleaner fuel used?

p: Book the charge with freight cost, paid by whoever pays freight under the Incoterm. Do not convert it into tonnes of CO2e. Your Scope 3 freight figure changes only if the carrier gives you shipment-level emissions that reflect the lower-intensity fuel, calculated under the GLEC Framework.
